description_full: MGIC Investment Corporation, through its subsidiaries, provides private mortgage insurance, other mortgage credit risk management solutions, and ancillary services in the United States, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and Guam. The company offers primary insurance that provides mortgage default protection on individual loans, as well as covers unpaid loan principal, delinquent interest, and various expenses associated with the default and subsequent foreclosure on the mortgage or sale of the underlying property. It also provides contract underwriting services, as well as reinsurance services. The company serves originators of residential mortgage loans, including savings institutions, commercial banks, mortgage brokers, credit unions, mortgage bankers, and other lenders. The company was founded in 1957 and is headquartered in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.

financial_summary: MGIC Investment Corporation is a mid-cap financial services business with a $5.5B market cap on $1.2B of annual revenue.

The top line has compounded at +1% over the past three years and +2% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory. Operating margins are expanding by +6.4pp year-over-year, which is one of the strongest signals that the moat is deepening.
Returns on capital run at 15% against a 8% cost of capital, a 7-point spread that creates value, though narrow enough that competitive pressure could close it.

The business throws off $852M in free cash flow — roughly 70 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.16× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 27× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 16.8% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and within its sector the business captures 3.0× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.
